quote: Transforming complex sentences into a sequence of shorter sentences, while preserving the original meaning, can facilitate the processing of complex texts for humans and machines alike. The results obtained in this comparative human evaluation are thus in line with those obtained on automated metrics overall, with marked improvements achieved via LLM-based SPRP. To gain further insights on the SPRP capabilities of LLMs, we performed an additional human evaluation, this time centred on assessing the validity of individual SPRP hypotheses on a set of predefined criteria. For this qualitative evaluation, we sampled 100 source sentences from Wiki-BM , a manually crafted benchmark created from Wikipedia data, and generated SPRP hypotheses with the Pythia-6.9B model fine-tuned on DeSSE data. The evaluation involved 8 human evaluators, who had to answer 6 questions related to the quality of an SPRP hypothesis considering a source sentence, addressing sencicality, grammaticality, deletion or introduction of new facts, correct splits and insufficient splits.

Evaluators compared hypotheses according to compliance, sensicality, grammaticality, missed facts and omitted facts (3‑way ranking); in the qualitative study they answered six specific questions about sensicality, grammaticality, missing facts, new facts, correct split and enough split.

An SPRP hypothesis can be considered correct if: it contains at least two separate sentences (compliance), it contains all the information in the source sentence (no missing facts), it does not contain information that was not present in the source sentence (no new facts), all the sentences in the hypothesis are grammatical (grammaticality), all the sentences in the hypothesis make sense both in isolation and in sequence (sensicality).
